papers.title: Early clinical outcomes of the PERIQxA multicentre randomised double-blind trial evaluating postoperative antibiotics after perianal abscess drainage
papers.authors: Polaino-Moreno V, Ruiz-Antorán B, Caballero-Bermejo A, Artés-Caselles M, Kraft M, Serrano-González J
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anal fistula frequently develops following surgical drainage of a first cryptoglandular perianal abscess. The role of postoperative antibiotics in preventing fistula formation remains uncertain.
METHODS: PERIQxA is a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluating postoperative amoxicillin-clavulanate compared with placebo after surgical drainage of a first cryptoglandular perianal abscess. This report presents early clinical outcomes from the ongoing trial. Adults without systemic infection or immunosuppression were randomised 1:1 to receive oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (875/125 mg) or placebo every 8 h for 7 days. The primary outcome was anal fistula formation at 6 months.
RESULTS: Between March 2022 and May 2025, 65 participants were randomised. One participant withdrew consent and was excluded from all analyses. Fifty-seven participants (28 antibiotic, 29 placebo) were included in the primary analysis. At 6 months, anal fistula developed in 21.4% of participants allocated to amoxicillin-clavulanate and 31.0% allocated to placebo (odds ratio [OR] 0.61, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.18-2.01). At 12 months, fistula formation occurred in 28.6% and 41.4% of participants, respectively (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.19-1.71). Lower rates of anal fistula formation were consistently observed in the antibiotic group at both time points, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Obesity (body mass index > 30 kg/m2) was associated with fistula formation. No antibiotic-related safety concerns were identified.
CONCLUSIONS: In this early analysis of the ongoing PERIQxA trial, lower rates of anal fistula formation were observed among participants allocated to postoperative amoxicillin-clavulanate compared with placebo at both 6 and 12 months of follow-up, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Given the limited sample size, these findings should be interpreted with caution and require confirmation. Additional evidence from PERIQxA, together with other ongoing randomised studies, will help clarify the role of postoperative antibiotic therapy in preventing anal fistula formation after perianal abscess drainage.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: EU Clinical Trials Information System, 2024-520193-35-00.

papers.title: Efficacy of erector spinae plane block for patients with inflammatory bowel disease undergoing major abdominal surgery: A double-blind randomized controlled trial
papers.authors: Alhamdah Y, Gleicher Y, Dos Santos Fernandes H, Peacock S, Ye X, Brown C
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) undergoing abdominal surgery face challenges in postoperative recovery due to high opioid needs and limited analgesic alternatives. The erector spinae plane (ESP) block has been shown to improve recovery in abdominal procedures, but its efficacy in the IBD population remains unknown. We investigated whether bilateral ESP blocks improve postoperative quality of recovery in this population.
METHODS: In this prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial, adults with IBD scheduled for elective laparoscopic-assisted abdominal surgery were randomized to receive bilateral ESP blocks with either 0.5% ropivacaine or normal saline before induction of anesthesia. The primary outcome was quality of recovery assessed using the 15-item QoR (QoR-15) scale at postoperative day (POD) 2. Secondary outcomes included QoR-15 at POD 1 and 3, pain scores (VAS), opioid consumption, opioid-related side effects, and hospital length of stay.
RESULTS: Fifty-seven patients were randomized and analyzed: 31 in the ropivacaine group and 26 in the saline group. Baseline characteristics were generally similar between groups. The postoperative QoR-15, defined as the average QoR-15 scores over POD 1-3, was 10.2 points higher in the intervention group although not statistically significant (p = 0.27). The intervention group had a smaller decline in postoperative QoR-15 scores compared to controls (mean difference in the change of postoperative QoR-15 from baseline = 19.9 points; 95% CI: 2.3 to 37.5; p = 0.02). Baseline-adjusted longitudinal analysis also suggested higher QoR-15 scores on POD 2 in the intervention group (28.9-point difference; 95% CI: 3.9 to 53.8; p = 0.02). However, these adjusted findings should be interpreted cautiously because the confidence intervals were wide, indicating limited precision. Pain scores and opioid consumption were similar between groups. Constipation was less frequent in the intervention group on POD 2 (p = 0.041). No significant differences were found in hospital length of stay.
CONCLUSION: The unadjusted primary comparison of postoperative QoR-15 at POD2 was not statistically significant; however, the intervention group scored numerically higher by 23 points, a substantial difference in magnitude that was consistent with the statistically significant effects observed in both change score and longitudinal mixed-effects analyses. Bilateral ESP blocks did not significantly reduce postoperative pain or opioid use. Taken together, these findings suggest a possible, clinically meaningful recovery benefit that should be considered exploratory and requires confirmation in larger multicenter trials with early postoperative analgesic assessment and block-success verification.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT06230003.

papers.title: Efficacy of novel compression gloves and stockings for prevention oxaliplatin induced peripheral neuropathy, the randomized controlled trial
papers.journal_full: Journal of the Egyptian National Cancer Institute
papers.authors: Leksuwankun S, Teeyapun N, Parinyanitikul N, Luangdilok S, Amornvit J, Teeramongkonrasmee A
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Given that oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy (OIPN) is a common and dose-limiting toxicity in colorectal cancer and that effective preventive strategies remain limited, this study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of compression therapy for the prevention of OIPN.
METHODS: We conducted a randomized controlled trial in patients with stage III colorectal cancer receiving oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, comparing pressure-controlled compression gloves and stockings during oxaliplatin infusion with usual care. The primary outcome was the incidence of grade ≥ 2 oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy (OIPN) assessed using NCI-CTCAE. Secondary outcomes included patient-reported neuropathy (EORTC QLQ-CIPN20), neuropathic pain (DN4), autonomic symptoms (Thai COMPASS-31), pain intensity (Wong-Baker Faces Pain Scale), and quantitative sensory testing. Longitudinal outcomes were analysed using mixed-effects models.
RESULTS: Twenty-five patients (17 compression, 8 control) were included in the final analysis. The incidence of grade ≥ 2 OIPN did not differ significantly between groups (17.6% vs. 25.0%, p = 1.00). However, the compression group demonstrated a significantly smaller increase in total CIPN20 scores compared with controls (median change 3.51 vs. 7.96; p = 0.04). Significant intervention-by-time interactions were observed for overall, sensory, and motor CIPN20 scores, as well as DN4 scores, indicating slower symptom progression with compression therapy. No significant differences were observed in autonomic symptoms, quantitative sensory testing, or pain intensity. There were no device-related adverse events.
CONCLUSION: Compression therapy did not significantly reduce clinician-graded OIPN but was associated with a trend toward slower progression of patient-reported neuropathy and neuropathic pain, supporting further evaluation in larger trials. (Thai Clinical Trials Registry: TCTR20221107006; registered 7 November 2022).

papers.title: Impact of a multicomponent health literacy intervention for general practitioners and patients on colorectal cancer screening in underserved areas in France-the DECODE pragmatic, cluster randomised controlled trial
papers.ptype: Randomized Controlled Trial, Pragmatic Clinical Trial
papers.authors: Redmond N, Lamouroux A, Fenni R, Addamiano M, Kaou M, Doukhi Z
papers.abstract: European colorectal cancer (CCR) screening programmes reduce mortality, yet participation in France remains low, particularly among individuals with limited health literacy (HL) and lower socioeconomic position. The DECODE trial assessed whether a combined HL intervention for General Practitioners (GPs) and eligible patients could improve CRC screening uptake after 1 year in French underserved areas. A two-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial in GP practices in underserved areas across four French regions was conducted. Practices were block-randomised (1:1) to intervention or usual care. The intervention combined HL-focussed interactive GP training with a patient-oriented pictorial brochure and video explaining the 'at-home' faecal immunochemical test (FIT). Patients aged 50-74 years, eligible for screening were recruited during routine consultations. Intervention GPs used their HL training to explain the FIT, and provided it alongside the patient-oriented materials; control arm GPs provided the FIT in their usual way. The primary outcome was FIT uptake at 1 year. Secondary outcomes, together with sociodemographic data, precarity, and HL levels, were examined. Mixed-effects logistic regression was performed accounting for clustering and baseline differences. Fifty-seven GPs (27 practices) were randomised and 1065 patients recruited (494 intervention, 571 control); 1022 were analysed. CRC screening uptake in the intervention arm (70.8%, 335/473) was increased compared to the control (64.5%, 354/549) (OR: 2.28, CI: 1.01-5.53, P = .046). No differences were observed for secondary outcomes. A multicomponent HL intervention targeting GP-patient interactions in underserved populations can improve CRC screening uptake within 1 year and may reduce related inequities, with future policy implications. Clinical trials registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, Trial registration number: 2020-A01687-32, Date of registration: 17th November 2020. URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT04631692. Protocol version: Manuscript based on study protocol version 1.3, 07 January 2022.

papers.title: Reimagining inflammatory bowel disease in the age of artificial intelligence: discovery, care, education, and sustainability for the next decade
papers.authors: Iacucci M, Zammarchi I, Pugliano C, Hanauer S, Peyrin-Biroulet L
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly evolving from task-specific algorithms to multimodal foundation models capable of integrating heterogeneous biological and clinical data across the health-care continuum. In inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), this transformation offers an unprecedented opportunity to move beyond fragmented analyses toward a unified understanding and management of disease. Artificial intelligence is emerging as the connective infrastructure linking scientific discovery, therapeutic development, patient care, education, and health-care delivery systems into continuously learning ecosystems. In this viewpoint, we explore how AI may reshape IBD over the next decade through 5 interconnected domains. Advances in multimodal AI accelerate biological discovery by integrating multiomics, spatial biology, and foundation models to identify mechanistic disease endotypes. Simultaneously, AI can shorten the path from molecular discovery to therapeutic innovation by supporting target identification, predicting protein structure, drug positioning, and adaptive clinical trial design. These scientific advances converge at the bedside, where multimodal AI may transform patient care from reactive management to predictive precision medicine through integrated diagnostics, digital biomarkers, real-time monitoring and individualized risk prediction. Beyond clinical care, AI is redefining medical education by enabling adaptive learning, explainable decision support, and democratized specialist expertise, while contributing to sustainable health care through optimized resource allocation, workforce support, and continuously learning systems. Realizing this vision will require robust governance, interoperability, prospective validation, and equitable implementation. If responsibly deployed, AI holds the potential to redefine IBD diagnosis, classification, therapeutic strategies and management within an intelligent ecosystem able to accelerate discovery, personalize care, and improve outcomes for patients and health-care systems alike.

papers.title: Melatonin as a multi-target modulator of chemoresistance in colorectal cancer: mechanistic insights and clinical perspectives
papers.authors: Vaghari-Tabari M, Mahrooz A, Yousefi B, Molavand M
papers.abstract: Chemoresistance in colorectal cancer (CRC) occurs for several major reasons, such as the enhancement of chemotherapy drug efflux and the attenuation of apoptosis. Enhanced efflux of chemotherapy drugs occurs due to increased expression and activity of ABC family transporters, especially ABCB1 (P-gp). The attenuation of apoptosis in colorectal cancer cells occurs for various reasons, such as enhanced antioxidant defense, enhanced DNA damage repair, and changes in the expression of apoptosis-related proteins. The enhancement of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and stemness and the dysregulation of cellular signaling pathways, such as PI3K/AKT, NF-κB, STAT3, and Wnt/β-catenin pathways, are also other important reasons for CRC chemoresistance. Interestingly, melatonin appears to attenuate chemoresistance in CRC cells. Numerous studies have demonstrated that melatonin influences nearly all key processes involved in CRC chemoresistance. Moreover, evidence from clinical studies suggesting the beneficial effects of melatonin in CRC chemotherapy is also available. In this article, we review the most interesting findings of all of these studies.

papers.title: Role of Bile Acids in Colorectal Diseases
papers.authors: Thirumal P, Azam M, Senthamizhselvan K
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Bile acids (BAs) have functions well beyond fat digestion. They also serve as signals linking the gut microbiota to gut health. This review examines how BAs affect colorectal diseases and how this knowledge can guide diagnosis and treatment.
RECENT FINDINGS: BAs and gut bacteria shape each other, and this balance affects the gut lining, immune system, and inflammation. Problems in BA handling are linked to bile acid diarrhea, post-cholecystectomy diarrhea, microscopic colitis, irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, and colorectal cancer. Ultra-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry and organoid models enable faster, more detailed BA testing. New treatments include BA binders, farnesoid X receptor-targeting drugs, and engineered gut bacteria. BAs play a central role in many colorectal diseases through their effects on gut bacteria and the gut lining. Better BA testing can improve diagnosis, and new BA- and microbiota-based treatments show promise. More studies are needed to bring these approaches into clinical practice.
